title: How a buy happens
one_liner: The sequence an agency follows from planning a purchase to explaining the award, and what a firm can read at each step.
why_here: Every route record assumes the reader knows which step a notice belongs to and who is acting at that step.

further_reading.title: GSA, How to Respond to Pre-Award Notices

self_check.q: Which step is used mainly to find capable small businesses before a solicitation is written?
self_check.explanation: GSA describes a sources-sought notice as "primarily used to identify small businesses capable of performing/providing the requirement" [572](#cite:572).

self_check.q: Outside commercial buys and above the simplified acquisition threshold, what is the minimum response time for offers?
self_check.explanation: FAR 5.203 allows at least a 30-day response time for actions exceeding the simplified acquisition threshold; the 15-day figure is the gap between notice and solicitation [563](#cite:563).

self_check.q: How long does an unsuccessful offeror have to ask in writing for a postaward debriefing?
options: 3 days after it receives notification of contract award
self_check.explanation: FAR 15.506 sets a written request within 3 days after the offeror received notification of contract award; the debriefing should occur within 5 days of the request [599](#cite:599).

body_before:
## What it is

Taken together, the [FAR](#term:far)'s parts describe a sequence without stating it in one place: plan, [forecast](#term:forecast), research the market, publish a notice, solicit, evaluate, award, [debrief](#term:debriefing) [1323](#cite:1323) [1324](#cite:1324) [562](#cite:562) [595](#cite:595) [599](#cite:599). 
Planning comes first: "Agencies shall perform [acquisition planning](#term:market-research) and conduct market research for all acquisitions." [1323](#cite:1323) Agencies with more than $50 million in annual contract actions prepare a forecast of expected opportunities, and [GSA](#term:gsa)'s governmentwide forecast tool needs no registration to search [579](#cite:579) [582](#cite:582). Market research then tests who could do the work, and a [sources-sought notice](#term:sources-sought) is, in GSA's words, "primarily used to identify small businesses capable of performing/providing the requirement" [1324](#cite:1324) [572](#cite:572).

The purchase then goes public. A proposed action over $25,000 is announced, or [synopsized](#term:synopsis), at [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov), the governmentwide point of entry [562](#cite:562) [418](#cite:418). Outside [commercial buys](#term:commercial-product) the notice appears at least 15 days before the [solicitation](#term:solicitation), and above the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) offerors get at least 30 days to respond [563](#cite:563). The method depends on the purchase: [Part 13](#term:simplified-acquisition-procedures) supplies simplified procedures up to that threshold, [Part 12](#term:far-part-12) applies when commercial products or services meet the need, and [Part 15](#term:far-part-15) governs negotiated buys [438](#cite:438) [442](#cite:442) [1325](#cite:1325). A Part 15 solicitation states the requirement and the evaluation factors with their relative importance, and a proposal received after the deadline is late [595](#cite:595).

Evaluation always includes price or cost, and a firm with no record "may not be evaluated favorably or unfavorably on [past performance](#term:cpars)" [596](#cite:596). A firm is registered in SAM when it offers and again at award [303](#cite:303). An unsuccessful offeror may ask in writing for a debriefing within 3 days of the [award notice](#term:sam-notice-codes); the debriefing covers the significant weaknesses or deficiencies in its proposal and does not compare offers point by point [599](#cite:599).

Several people act along the way. The [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) decides whether the purchase is [set aside](#term:set-aside) and designates the industry code that fixes the [size standard](#term:size-standard) [384](#cite:384) [285](#cite:285). The agency's [small business specialist](#term:osdbu) is consulted no later than 30 days before a solicitation, and [SBA](#term:sba)'s [procurement center representative](#term:pcr) recommends set-asides within 15 days of receiving an acquisition package [428](#cite:428) [430](#cite:430). Once the solicitation is out, "the contracting officer must be the focal point of any exchange with potential offerors" [590](#cite:590).
picture:
Draw a horizontal timeline with nine stations: plan, forecast, market research, sources sought, synopsis, solicitation, evaluation, award, debrief. Under each station sits the FAR part that governs it: Part 7 under plan, Part 10 under market research, Part 5 under synopsis, Parts 12, 13 or 15 under solicitation and evaluation, and [Part 19](#term:far-part-19) running the full length as the small-business thread [1323](#cite:1323) [1324](#cite:1324) [562](#cite:562) [442](#cite:442) [438](#cite:438) [1325](#cite:1325) [384](#cite:384).

Two gaps carry their minimum lengths: 15 days from notice to solicitation, and 30 days from solicitation to offers above the simplified acquisition threshold [563](#cite:563). A third, after award, reads *3 days to ask for a debriefing* [599](#cite:599). Above the line, small figures mark who acts: the contracting officer throughout, the small business specialist and the procurement center representative before the solicitation [428](#cite:428) [430](#cite:430). A dotted bracket from the first station to the receipt of proposals is labelled *exchanges with industry encouraged* [590](#cite:590).
body_after:
## How this guide uses it

Chapter 2 walks the same sequence with its thresholds, and chapter 3 sets it beside the defense pathways and the [grants](#term:grant) model. The mechanics records for reading SAM.gov, for market research from the firm's side and for responding cover the stations a firm can see. The route records name the step at which each route opens.


The section numbers here are those of the codified FAR. Agencies that adopted the overhaul's model text use new ones: early exchanges with industry move from 15.201 to 15.101, and postaward debriefings from 15.506 to 15.301-1 [577](#cite:577). A [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) of June 23, 2026 would codify the overhaul of Part 5, the part on publicizing; it is not final [574](#cite:574).

title: Other transactions 101
one_liner: An other transaction is a binding agreement that is not a procurement contract, grant or cooperative agreement, used mostly for defense research and prototypes.
why_here: A whole route family in this guide runs outside the FAR, with its own conditions, solicitations and consortium membership.

further_reading.title: GAO-22-105357, DOD Can Improve Planning for Consortia Awards

self_check.q: Which of these is one of the four statutory conditions for a DoD prototype OT?
options: The firm holds a GSA Schedule contract
At least one third of the total cost is paid from non-Federal sources
The agreement is worth less than $350,000
The firm is registered on Grants.gov
self_check.explanation: 10 U.S.C. 4022(d)(1) lists four alternatives: significant participation by a nontraditional defense contractor or nonprofit research institution, all significant participants small or nontraditional, one third of total cost from non-Federal sources, or a written finding of exceptional circumstances [1028](#cite:1028).

self_check.q: Which type of OT carries no authority for follow-on production?
options: Any OT awarded through a consortium
self_check.explanation: DoD's research OT page says research OTs "do not include authority for follow-on production contracts or transactions" [1055](#cite:1055).

self_check.q: In a consortium OT, who issues the project sub-award to the member that performs the work?
options: A contracting officer under FAR Part 15
self_check.explanation: GAO describes the consortium management organization issuing "a project sub-award—which executes the project—to the consortium member" after DoD selects the member [1119](#cite:1119).

body_before:
## What it is

An [other transaction (OT)](#term:other-transaction) is a legally binding instrument that is not a standard [procurement contract](#term:grant), grant or cooperative agreement [1053](#cite:1053). The [FAR](#term:far) does not automatically apply to it; the Procurement Integrity Act and fiscal law still do [1053](#cite:1053). DARPA's training lists what falls away: the Competition in Contracting Act, the [Truth in Negotiations Act](#term:certified-cost-or-pricing-data), [Cost Accounting Standards](#term:cost-accounting-standards), the [Contract Disputes Act](#term:contract-disputes-act), the [protest](#term:bid-protest) process, and the FAR and [DFARS](#term:dfars). Criminal law and export control remain [1063](#cite:1063). Intellectual property follows the agreement: "Rights need to be specifically stated in the agreement." [1064](#cite:1064)

DoD's guide names three types [1049](#cite:1049). A [research OT](#term:research-ot) (10 U.S.C. 4021) funds basic, applied and advanced research, expects the other parties to match Government funds where practicable, and carries no authority for [follow-on production](#term:follow-on-production) [1031](#cite:1031) [1055](#cite:1055). A [prototype OT](#term:prototype-ot) (10 U.S.C. 4022) needs one of four conditions: a [nontraditional defense contractor](#term:nontraditional-defense-contractor) or [nonprofit research institution](#term:sttr) participating to a significant extent; all significant participants [being small](#term:size-standard) businesses or nontraditional defense contractors; at least [one third of the cost](#term:cost-share) paid from non-Federal sources; or a written finding of exceptional circumstances [1028](#cite:1028). A production OT follows a prototype project that was competitively awarded and successfully completed, and may go to its participants without further competition [1029](#cite:1029).

A [commercial solutions opening (CSO)](#term:cso) is a general [solicitation](#term:solicitation) that "may be structured as prototype OTs pursuant to 10 U.S.C. 4022, or as FAR-based contracts or agreements pursuant to 10 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 3458/DFARS 212.70" [1058](#cite:1058). A [broad agency announcement (BAA)](#term:baa) covers basic and applied research not tied to a specific system, and DoD's comparison page says it "Cannot be used for production" [271](#cite:271) [1057](#cite:1057). The CSO statute dropped its "innovative" limit on December 18, 2025; DFARS Subpart 212.70 has not [1033](#cite:1033) [806](#cite:806) [1040](#cite:1040).

DoD awards a [base agreement](#term:base-agreement) to a [consortium management organization](#term:consortium-manager) and selects the member that will do the work; the manager issues a project sub-award to that member, and the base agreement is the starting point for negotiating it [1119](#cite:1119). [GAO](#term:gao) reports that "Consortia-based OTAs account for half of [DOD](#term:department-of-war)'s prototype OTA obligations from [fiscal years](#term:fiscal-year) 2021 to 2024" [1121](#cite:1121). For most [consortia](#term:consortium), members pay dues and gain exclusive access to the Government's opportunities [1119](#cite:1119).
picture:
Draw a fork that reads left to right. Three doors stand on the left: *CSO*, *consortium request* and *BAA* [1058](#cite:1058) [1119](#cite:1119) [271](#cite:271). The CSO door has a side exit, *FAR-based contract* [1058](#cite:1058). The first two doors lead to a central box, *prototype OT*, behind a gate with four leaves: a nontraditional or nonprofit participant, all participants small or nontraditional, one-third cost share, exceptional circumstances. Any one leaf opens it [1028](#cite:1028).

From the prototype box an arrow labelled *competitively awarded and successfully completed* runs right to *follow-on production* [1029](#cite:1029). The BAA door leads to a *research* box marked *no production*; the research OT sits there too, with no arrow onward [1057](#cite:1057) [1055](#cite:1055). Inside the consortium door sits a short chain: Government, base agreement, manager, project agreement, member [1119](#cite:1119). A sidebar lists what does not apply [1063](#cite:1063).
body_after:
## The maths, gently

$$ P \ge \tfrac{1}{3}\,T $$

- *T* is the total cost of the prototype project and *P* is the part paid from sources other than the Federal Government; this is the third of the four conditions [1028](#cite:1028).
- Worked, with illustrative figures: on a project with a total cost of $3,000,000, the condition is met when at least $1,000,000 comes from non-Federal sources [1028](#cite:1028).
- The share is one alternative among four, so a project that meets the first or second condition needs no cost share [1028](#cite:1028).

## How this guide uses it

The route records for the prototype OT, the research OT, follow-on production, the defense commercial solutions opening, the broad agency announcement and consortium membership open from this picture, as do the civilian OT routes. The OT gates cover approvals, intellectual property, protests, disputes, cost share and the consortium project agreement.


The certification record for nontraditional defense contractor status explains the term in the first two conditions: no DoD contract or [subcontract](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) under full cost accounting standards coverage in the year before the solicitation [1032](#cite:1032).

title: Partnering forms 101
one_liner: Six ways to work with another firm on federal work, each with its own answer on size, work share and payment.
why_here: The partnering routes look alike from outside but carry different size, work-share and payment rules.

further_reading.title: GAO-22-105357, DOD Can Improve Planning for Consortia Awards

self_check.q: In a mentor-protégé joint venture on a set-aside, what is the least share of the venture's work the protégé performs?
self_check.explanation: 13 CFR 125.8 has the protégé perform at least 40% of the work performed by the joint venture; 51% is the ownership figure for a separate-legal-entity venture [773](#cite:773).

self_check.q: On a GSA Schedule contractor team arrangement responding to a small-business set-aside order, who has to be small?
options: Only members doing more than half the work
No one; Schedule orders are never set aside
self_check.explanation: GSA's guidance says all members must be small for the arrangement to be eligible for a small-business set-aside order [763](#cite:763) [762](#cite:762).

self_check.q: A small prime on a set-aside relies on a subcontractor that is not similarly situated to do the primary and vital work. What follows under 13 CFR 121.103(h)?
options: The team is treated as a joint venture
Nothing, provided the arrangement is disclosed
The offeror is ineligible as a small business
self_check.explanation: That subcontractor is an ostensible subcontractor [706](#cite:706); since the rule effective January 16, 2025 the offeror is ineligible as small and is no longer treated as a joint venture [292](#cite:292).

body_before:
## What it is

A firm can do federal work with another firm in six forms. The plainest is the [subcontract](#term:prime-and-subcontractor): subcontractors "do not work directly with the government, but instead work for other contractors" [730](#cite:730). A prime that is not small holds a [subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan) on a contract expected to exceed $900,000 ($2 million for construction) [692](#cite:692). The subcontractor is small as of the date it certifies for that subcontract, under the [NAICS code](#term:naics) the prime picks [986](#cite:986) [989](#cite:989). Payment reaches it through the prime: the Government pays the prime by the later of the 30th day after a [proper invoice](#term:prompt-payment) or after acceptance, and a prime paid early pays its small-business subcontractors "within 15 days after receipt of [accelerated payments](#term:accelerated-payment) from the Government" [941](#cite:941) [661](#cite:661).

Two forms are teams. Under [FAR](#term:far) subpart 9.6 a prime agrees with other companies to act as its subcontractors on a specified contract, the arrangement is disclosed in the offer, and the prime stays fully responsible [761](#cite:761). On a [set-aside](#term:set-aside) the team meets the [ostensible subcontractor rule](#term:ostensible-subcontractor): if a subcontractor that is not [similarly situated](#term:similarly-situated-entity) performs the primary and vital work, or the prime is unusually reliant on it, the offeror is ineligible as small [706](#cite:706) [292](#cite:292). A [GSA Schedule](#term:mas) [contractor team arrangement (CTA)](#term:cta) differs. Each member holds its own Schedule contract and acts as prime for its share, and all members must be small for a set-aside order [762](#cite:762) [763](#cite:763).

Two forms are [joint ventures](#term:joint-venture). A joint venture is in writing, does business under its own name and is identified in [SAM](#term:sam-gov); it is small if each partner is small, and it generally may not be awarded contracts beyond two years from its first award [770](#cite:770). A [mentor-protégé](#term:mentor-protege-sba) joint venture is small wherever the protégé alone is small, once [SBA](#term:sba) has approved the mentor-protégé agreement [785](#cite:785). Its agreement makes the protégé managing venturer, with at least 51% of a separate-legal-entity venture and at least 40% of the venture's work [773](#cite:773).

The sixth form, [consortium membership](#term:consortium), belongs to [other transactions](#term:other-transaction). For most consortia members pay dues; DoD selects the member, and the [consortium manager](#term:consortium-manager) issues it the [project sub-award](#term:base-agreement) [1119](#cite:1119).
picture:
Draw a grid: six rows for the forms and three columns for the questions, who counts as small, who does the work and who pays the small firm.


Subcontract: the subcontractor, at certification; as the subcontract says; the prime [986](#cite:986) [661](#cite:661). FAR 9.6 team: the prime, with no ostensible subcontractor; prime and named subcontractors; the prime [761](#cite:761) [706](#cite:706). Schedule CTA: every member; each its own share; as the team's agreement sets out, each member having privity with the Government [762](#cite:762) [763](#cite:763). Joint venture: every partner; the partners in aggregate; the contract holder, which is the venture or, for an informal venture, the small partner [770](#cite:770) [423](#cite:423) [773](#cite:773). Mentor-protégé joint venture: the protégé; the protégé at least 40%; a special bank account in the venture's name [785](#cite:785) [773](#cite:773). Consortium: size is not the test, one of the four prototype conditions is; the selected member; the manager, by sub-award [1028](#cite:1028) [1119](#cite:1119).
body_after:
## The maths, gently

$$ W_{p} \ge 0.40 \times W_{jv} $$

- *W* with the subscript *jv* is the work the joint venture itself performs, and *W* with the subscript *p* is the protégé's part of it [773](#cite:773).
- Worked, with illustrative figures: if the venture performs $600,000 of work, the protégé performs at least 0.40 × $600,000 = $240,000 [773](#cite:773).
- Ownership runs the other way: the protégé holds at least 51% of a separate-legal-entity venture, and the mentor may hold up to 40% of the protégé firm itself [773](#cite:773) [785](#cite:785).

## How this guide uses it

Chapter 6 takes the six forms in turn, and each has a route record. The gates cover the ostensible subcontractor rule, joint venture agreements, the [limitations on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting), payment, disputes with a prime and [past performance](#term:cpars) as a subcontractor.


One limit runs through the subcontract and the FAR 9.6 team: the subcontractor has no contract with the Government [976](#cite:976) [979](#cite:979). [GAO](#term:gao) "will not consider a [protest](#term:bid-protest) of the award or proposed award of a subcontract" [467](#cite:467).

title: Reading a SAM.gov notice
one_liner: A SAM.gov notice is a short record: a type code, a set-aside code, an industry code, an active flag and a response deadline.
why_here: The guide's opportunity search shows these fields, and SBIR topics, grants and consortium requests are published elsewhere.

further_reading.title: GSA, SAM.gov Get Opportunities Public API
FAR 5.207, Preparation and transmittal of synopses

self_check.q: Which of these is a notice-type code in the SAM.gov public API?
self_check.explanation: The API documentation lists nine type codes, among them r for Sources Sought; RFI is not one of them [567](#cite:567).

self_check.q: What does active: No mean on a notice?
options: The firm viewing it is not registered
self_check.explanation: In the API documentation, active Yes means an active opportunity and No means an archived one [567](#cite:567).

self_check.q: Where is a Department of War SBIR or STTR proposal submitted?
options: By email to the contracting officer
self_check.explanation: The department's opportunities page says all of its SBIR and STTR proposals must be submitted electronically through the Defense SBIR/STTR Innovation Portal (DSIP) [52](#cite:52).

body_before:
## What it is

[SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) is the governmentwide point of entry, the single place where federal business opportunities greater than $25,000 can be reached by the public [418](#cite:418). The site's own definition is short: "Contract opportunities are procurement notices from federal contracting offices." [569](#cite:569) Anyone can search them without an account [569](#cite:569). Each notice carries one of nine type codes: p for [presolicitation](#term:presolicitation), r for [sources sought](#term:sources-sought), s for [special notice](#term:sam-notice-codes), o for [solicitation](#term:solicitation), k for [combined synopsis/solicitation](#term:combined-synopsis-solicitation), a for award notice, u for justification, g for sale of surplus property and i for intent to bundle [567](#cite:567). "[RFI](#term:rfi)" is not among them [567](#cite:567).

Four more fields do most of the work. The [set-aside](#term:set-aside) field holds one of eighteen codes, among them [SBA](#term:sba), SBP, 8A, HZC, SDVOSBC, [WOSB](#term:wosb) and EDWOSB; this guide reads SBA as a total small-business set-aside and SBP as a partial one, readings that are its own and are flagged for checking against the API page [567](#cite:567). The [FAR](#term:far) requires the [synopsis](#term:synopsis) to identify the type of set-aside [565](#cite:565). The [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) assigns one [NAICS code](#term:naics) by principal purpose, and that code fixes the [size standard](#term:size-standard) [425](#cite:425) [285](#cite:285). The `active` flag reads Yes for an active opportunity and No for an archived one, and `responseDeadLine` gives the date responses are due [567](#cite:567).

The deadlines follow rules. Outside [commercial buys](#term:commercial-product), a notice appears at least 15 days before the solicitation; above the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) offerors get at least 30 days to respond, and at least 45 days for research and development [563](#cite:563). SAM.gov names three ways to take the data in bulk: DataBank reports, downloadable contract opportunity data files, and a public API [569](#cite:569). The data.gov record for the downloadable file, the daily extract this guide's search draws on, does not state how often the file is updated [571](#cite:571).

Not every opportunity is here. Defense [SBIR](#term:sbir) and [STTR](#term:sttr) proposals go only through the [DSIP portal](#term:dsip), and [SBIR.gov](#term:sbir-gov) aggregates agency solicitation information [52](#cite:52) [11](#cite:11). [Grant](#term:grant) [notices of funding opportunity](#term:nofo) are posted on [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) and generally stay open at least 60 calendar days [1328](#cite:1328). DoD's guide says SAM.gov may not be the most appropriate place to advertise [other transactions](#term:other-transaction), and for most [consortia](#term:consortium) members pay dues and gain exclusive access to the Government's opportunities [1049](#cite:1049) [1119](#cite:1119).
picture:
Draw one notice as an annotated card. A header strip holds the title and the contracting office. Six callouts point at the fields: the type code, with a miniature timeline that places r, p, o or k, and a along the buying sequence; the set-aside code; the NAICS code, with an arrow to *size standard*; the active flag; the response deadline, drawn as a countdown; and the contact point and place of performance [567](#cite:567) [565](#cite:565).

Beside the card sit three smaller, greyed cards for what SAM.gov contract opportunities do not carry: *SBIR topic: DSIP or the agency's own site*, *grant: Grants.gov*, and *other transaction: consortium request* [52](#cite:52) [1328](#cite:1328) [1119](#cite:1119).
body_after:
## The maths, gently

$$ t_{\text{offers due}} - t_{\text{notice}} \;\ge\; 15 + 30 = 45 \text{ days} $$

- Each *t* is a date. For a non-commercial action above the simplified acquisition threshold, the two minimums add up when the response time runs from the solicitation, as the overhaul's Part 5 table states it: 15 days from notice to solicitation, then 30 days to respond [563](#cite:563) [573](#cite:573).
- For research and development above that threshold the response time is at least 45 days, so the sum is 15 + 45 = 60 days [563](#cite:563).

## How this guide uses it

The mechanics record for reading SAM.gov contract opportunities lists every type code and set-aside code, and the opportunity search filters on the fields described here. The program records for SBIR, grants and consortia point to the portals where those opportunities appear.


The citations here are to the codified FAR. The overhaul's model text for Part 5 requires a presolicitation notice above $20,000 and keeps the 15-day and 30-day figures; a [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) of June 23, 2026 would codify it and is not final [573](#cite:573) [574](#cite:574).

title: SBIR phases 101
one_liner: SBIR and STTR fund a small firm's own research in phases; only the first two draw on the reserved money.
why_here: The research-funding routes in this guide are built on these phases, and the April 2026 act changed several of their rules.

further_reading.title: Public Law 119-83, Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act

self_check.q: Which phase is paid from funds other than the SBIR/STTR set-aside and has no dollar limit in SBA's directive?
self_check.explanation: The Policy Directive defines Phase III as work that derives from, extends or completes earlier SBIR/STTR work, funded from non-SBIR/STTR sources, with no limit on number, duration, type or dollar value [5](#cite:5).

self_check.q: In STTR, what is the least share of the work the small firm itself performs?
self_check.explanation: The directive requires not less than 40 percent of the work by the small business and not less than 30 percent by the research institution [5](#cite:5).

self_check.q: How long is SBIR/STTR data protected under DFARS 252.227-7018, and what does FAR 52.227-20 still say?
self_check.explanation: The defense clause runs 20 years from contract award [24](#cite:24); the civilian clause, dated May 2014, still states a period of 4 years [25](#cite:25).

body_before:
## What it is

[SBIR](#term:sbir) and [STTR](#term:sttr) pay small firms to research and develop their own technology. Agencies with large extramural research budgets must spend not less than 3.2 percent of them on SBIR and 0.45 percent on STTR [3](#cite:3). An awardee, together with its [affiliates](#term:affiliation), must not have more than 500 employees [10](#cite:10). [SBIR.gov](#term:sbir-gov) lists eleven participating agencies, six of them with STTR, and the rules sit in 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 638 and [SBA](#term:sba)'s [Policy Directive](#term:policy-directive) effective May 3, 2023 [12](#cite:12) [3](#cite:3) [5](#cite:5).

[Phase I](#term:phase-i) is feasibility work, normally not more than 6 months for SBIR or 1 year for STTR, with a base guideline of $150,000; Phase II continues it, normally for not more than 2 years, with a guideline of $1,000,000 [5](#cite:5). As of April 2026 agencies may go to $323,090 and $2,153,927 without SBA approval [11](#cite:11). [Direct to Phase II](#term:direct-to-phase-ii) lets named agencies award a [Phase II](#term:phase-ii) with no Phase I before it, on a written determination of demonstrated feasibility [5](#cite:5).

[Phase III](#term:phase-iii) is work that derives from, extends or completes earlier SBIR/STTR work, paid from other funds. The directive says "There is no limit on the number, duration, type, or dollar value of Phase III awards made to a business concern", and the Phase I and II size limits do not apply [5](#cite:5). An agency may award it [sole source](#term:sole-source) with no [FAR Part 6](#term:full-and-open-competition) justification and no [FAR](#term:far) Part 5 notice [225](#cite:225). [Data rights](#term:sbir-data-rights) depend on the [clause](#term:clause-numbering): SBA's directive and the defense clause [DFARS](#term:dfars) 252.227-7018 protect SBIR/STTR data for 20 years from award, while the civilian clause FAR 52.227-20 still says 4 years [5](#cite:5) [24](#cite:24) [25](#cite:25).

The instrument varies by agency. SBA's agency cards show [grants](#term:grant) at [USDA](#term:agency-abbreviations), Commerce and NSF, contracts at Education, DHS, DOT, EPA and NASA, both at HHS, and "Agreements" at DOE [12](#cite:12). Authority lapsed after September 30, 2025; [Pub. L. 119-83](#term:sbir-reauthorization-2026), approved April 13, 2026, restored the programs through September 30, 2031 [3](#cite:3) [1](#cite:1). The act adds a [Strategic Breakthrough award](#term:strategic-breakthrough-award) of not more than $30,000,000 over not more than 48 months, extends Direct to Phase II to the Department of Energy, NASA and STTR, and has each agency set a per-firm proposal limit from [fiscal year](#term:fiscal-year) 2027 [1](#cite:1).

Step two is *Phase II: guideline $1,000,000, ceiling $2,153,927* [5](#cite:5) [11](#cite:11). A bypass arrow from the ground to step two is labelled *Direct to Phase II* [5](#cite:5). ## The maths, gently

$$ \text{SBIR} \ge 0.032 \times B \qquad \text{STTR} \ge 0.0045 \times B $$

- *B* is an agency's extramural research budget. The SBIR share applies above $100,000,000 and the STTR share above $1,000,000,000 [3](#cite:3).
- Worked, with an illustrative budget of $2,000,000,000: at least 0.032 × $2,000,000,000 = $64,000,000 for SBIR and 0.0045 × $2,000,000,000 = $9,000,000 for STTR [3](#cite:3).
- STTR work share: the firm performs not less than 40 percent and the research institution not less than 30 percent [5](#cite:5).

## How this guide uses it

Chapter 5 follows the phases. The program records give each agency's amounts, dates and portal, and separate records cover Direct to Phase II, Strategic Breakthrough awards and Phase III. The gates cover registration, data-rights marking, proposal limits and security review.


Several of the act's measures are pending. SBA is to modify the policy directives within one year of enactment, which is April 13, 2027, and SBIR.gov still posts the May 2023 directive [1](#cite:1) [7](#cite:7). A rule proposed in 2023 would change the 4 years in FAR 52.227-20 to 20; it is not final [228](#cite:228).

body_before:
## What it is

In federal contracting, small is a measured status. A [size standard](#term:size-standard) is a ceiling for one [NAICS](#term:naics) industry code, set in employees or in average annual receipts, and the table of ceilings is 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 121.201 [284](#cite:284). The [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) designates the code for each [solicitation](#term:solicitation), and "A concern must not exceed the size standard for the NAICS code specified in the solicitation." [285](#cite:285)

The measurement is an average. Receipts are averaged over the latest five completed [fiscal years](#term:fiscal-year). Employees are averaged over the preceding 24 calendar months, and "Part-time and temporary employees are counted the same as full-time employees." [281](#cite:281) [282](#cite:282) Size is fixed on the date of the firm's written [self-certification](#term:representations-and-certifications) with its initial offer that includes price, and a firm that is small at award generally stays small for the life of the contract [290](#cite:290).

[Affiliation](#term:affiliation) decides whose numbers count. [SBA](#term:sba)'s guide puts it in one sentence: "Affiliation with another business is based on the power to control, whether exercised or not." [278](#cite:278) Affiliates' employees and receipts are added to the firm's own [278](#cite:278). Control can come from ownership, common management or family ties, and economic dependence is presumed when 70% or more of a firm's receipts come from one concern over three fiscal years [297](#cite:297). The exceptions in 13 CFR 121.103(b) include firms owned by [Indian Tribes](#term:entity-owned-firm), Alaska Native Corporations, Native Hawaiian Organizations and Community Development Corporations, and SBA-approved [mentor-protégé](#term:mentor-protege-sba) relationships [297](#cite:297).

Status can change and be challenged. 13 CFR 125.12 requires [recertification](#term:recertification) within 30 calendar days of a merger, acquisition or sale that changes controlling interest, and on contracts longer than five years [291](#cite:291). A competitor's [size protest](#term:size-protest) is due by the fifth business day after bid opening or notice of the apparent successful offeror, and the same deadline applies to [HUBZone](#term:hubzone), [SDVOSB](#term:sdvosb) and [WOSB](#term:wosb) status protests [294](#cite:294) [458](#cite:458) [462](#cite:462) [463](#cite:463) [464](#cite:464). Willful misrepresentation of size carries "a presumption of loss to the United States based on the total amount expended" [295](#cite:295) [296](#cite:296).
picture:
Draw a decision flow of four boxes, left to right. Box one asks which NAICS code is on the solicitation [285](#cite:285). Box two asks whether that code's ceiling is in receipts or in employees [284](#cite:284). Box three, *add affiliates*, holds a small sketch: the firm in the centre, solid lines to an owner, a sister company and a dominant customer, each labelled *control*, and two dashed lines labelled *exception* to an approved mentor and to a Tribal owner [297](#cite:297).

Box four compares the total with the ceiling on the date of the first priced offer [290](#cite:290). Two markers hang off the flow. A loop arrow from *merger, acquisition or sale* returns to box three, labelled *recertify within 30 calendar days* [291](#cite:291). A flag on box four reads *[protest](#term:bid-protest): fifth business day* [294](#cite:294).

## The maths, gently

$$ \frac{R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + R_4 + R_5}{5} + A \le S $$

- *R₁* to *R₅* are the firm's receipts in its latest five completed fiscal years, *A* is the same average for its affiliates, and *S* is the ceiling for the solicitation's NAICS code [281](#cite:281) [278](#cite:278) [285](#cite:285).
- Worked, with illustrative figures: receipts of $4, $5, $6, $7 and $8 million average $6 million. With one affiliate averaging $3 million, the figure compared with the ceiling is $9 million [281](#cite:281) [278](#cite:278).
- Economic dependence: when the share of receipts from one concern is 0.70 or more over three fiscal years, affiliation is presumed, and the presumption can be rebutted [297](#cite:297).

## How this guide uses it

Chapter 4 opens with this test. The certification records for size standards and for affiliation carry the full rules, and the gates for representing size and for recertification apply them. The size protest and status protest routes cover the challenges, and the [joint venture](#term:joint-venture) and mentor-protégé records rest on the affiliation exceptions.


[SBIR](#term:sbir) and [STTR](#term:sttr) use their own test: an awardee, together with its affiliates, must not have more than 500 employees [10](#cite:10). Pending: a [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) of August 20, 2026 would collapse nearly 1,000 size standards into 338; comments closed September 21, 2026 and it has no effective date [288](#cite:288).

body_before:
## What it is

A [set-aside](#term:set-aside) is a purchase that the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) restricts to small businesses. The test is called the [rule of two](#term:rule-of-two): the purchase is restricted when offers are reasonably expected from two or more small firms [384](#cite:384). A firm claims the status by representing its size in writing with its initial offer [427](#cite:427).

Two dollar lines sort the rule. Since October 1, 2025 the [micro-purchase threshold](#term:micro-purchase-threshold) is $15,000 and the simplified acquisition threshold is $350,000 [417](#cite:417). Between them a purchase is set aside unless the contracting officer finds no reasonable expectation of offers from two or more small businesses, and statute reserves the same band [384](#cite:384) [374](#cite:374). Above $350,000 the purchase is set aside when offers are expected from at least two [responsible small businesses](#term:responsibility) and award will be at fair market prices [384](#cite:384).

Four certified programs sit beside the general set-aside: [8(a)](#term:eight-a), [HUBZone](#term:hubzone), [service-disabled veteran-owned](#term:sdvosb) (SDVOSB) and [women-owned](#term:wosb) (WOSB). Above the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) they are considered before a general small-business set-aside, with no order of precedence among them [429](#cite:429). Each also allows a [sole-source award](#term:sole-source), one made without competition below a dollar ceiling. The codified [FAR](#term:far) puts that ceiling at $8.5 million for manufacturing industry codes and $5.5 million otherwise for 8(a), HUBZone and WOSB, and at $8.5 million and $5 million for SDVOSB [338](#cite:338) [349](#cite:349) [357](#cite:357) [368](#cite:368). [SBA](#term:sba)'s own rule still prints $7,000,000 and $4,500,000 for 8(a) [331](#cite:331).

Orders are a separate case. Under a [multiple-award contract](#term:idiq), setting an order aside is at the contracting officer's discretion [420](#cite:420) [431](#cite:431). An SBA rule proposed in October 2024 would apply the rule of two to orders; no [final rule](#term:final-rule) was found [472](#cite:472). A set-aside also carries a condition: on a services set-aside above the simplified acquisition threshold, the small prime may pay no more than 50 percent of what the Government pays it to [subcontractors](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) that are not [similarly situated](#term:similarly-situated-entity) [422](#cite:422).
picture:
Draw a ladder with three rungs, read upward by purchase value. Rung one, up to $15,000, is the micro-purchase, where the purchase card is the preferred method [417] [440]. Rung two, above $15,000 and up to $350,000, is reserved for small business unless two competitive offers cannot be expected [384](#cite:384).

Rung three, above $350,000 [417](#cite:417), holds two diamonds. The first asks whether one of the four certified programs fits; the second asks whether two responsible small firms are expected at fair market prices. A yes at either leads to a set-aside box; two noes lead to a box marked *not set aside* [429](#cite:429) [384](#cite:384). A side rail labelled *sole source* runs beside rungs two and three and stops at each program's ceiling [338](#cite:338) [368](#cite:368). A smaller ladder for orders under multiple-award contracts carries one label, *discretionary* [420](#cite:420).

## The maths, gently

$$ \$15{,}000 < V \le \$350{,}000 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{set aside unless } N < 2 $$

$$ V > \$350{,}000 \text{ and } N \ge 2 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{set aside} $$

- *V* is the expected value of the purchase and *N* is the number of small firms the contracting officer reasonably expects to offer [384](#cite:384) [417](#cite:417).
- Sole source outside manufacturing: the FAR line for 8(a) is $5.5 million and the line printed in 13 CFR 124.506 is $4,500,000, so an illustrative $5,000,000 requirement falls under one official text and over the other [338](#cite:338) [331](#cite:331).
- [Limitation on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting), services: on an illustrative $400,000 set-aside, at most 0.50 × $400,000 = $200,000 may go to subcontractors that are not similarly situated [422](#cite:422) [423](#cite:423).

## How this guide uses it

The route records for the total small-business set-aside, the partial set-aside, the order set-aside and the four program routes all rest on this idea. So do the gates for representing size, the limitations on subcontracting and the [nonmanufacturer rule](#term:nonmanufacturer-rule). Chapter 2 places the rule of two in the buying sequence and chapter 4 covers the certifications.


The section numbers here are those of the codified FAR. Agencies that adopted the overhaul's model text, [GSA](#term:gsa) from November 3, 2025 and DoD from February 1, 2026, find the rule of two stated once, at 19.104-1 [391](#cite:391) [400](#cite:400) [402](#cite:402).

body_before:
## What it is

A federal contracting number has an address, and usually more than one. Statute comes first: the small business goals and the reserved band are in 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 644, [SBIR](#term:sbir) and [STTR](#term:sttr) in 15 U.S.C. 638, and the [prototype other transaction](#term:prototype-ot) in 10 U.S.C. 4022 [374](#cite:374) [3](#cite:3) [1028](#cite:1028). Regulation implements statute: the [Federal Acquisition Regulation](#term:far), whose pages on acquisition.gov show the circular they are current to ([FAC](#term:fac) 2026-01, effective 03/13/2026), and [SBA](#term:sba)'s rules in Title 13 of the [Code of Federal Regulations](#term:cfr) [418](#cite:418) [331](#cite:331). Below both sit [policy directives](#term:policy-directive), [class deviations](#term:class-deviation) and agency pages [5](#cite:5) [400](#cite:400) [310](#cite:310).

A number changes by a dated document. The [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) went from $250,000 to $350,000, and the [micro-purchase threshold](#term:micro-purchase-threshold) from $10,000 to $15,000, by a [final rule](#term:final-rule) in the [Federal Register](#term:federal-register) (90 FR 41872) effective October 1, 2025 [340](#cite:340) [417](#cite:417). The same rule moved the subcontracting-plan threshold from $750,000 to $900,000 [340](#cite:340).

The FAR itself now exists in two numberings. [Executive Order](#term:executive-order) 14275 of April 15, 2025 ordered a rewrite, and agencies adopt the rewritten model text part by part through class deviations: for [Part 19](#term:far-part-19), [GSA](#term:gsa) from November 3, 2025 and DoD from February 1, 2026 [386](#cite:386) [400](#cite:400) [402](#cite:402). The codified text stays in force beside it. The [rule of two](#term:rule-of-two) is at 19.502-2 in the codified FAR and at 19.104-1 in the model text [384](#cite:384) [391](#cite:391). The first [proposed rules](#term:proposed-rule) to codify the rewrite appeared on June 23, 2026 [403](#cite:403).

The layers do not update together, so pages disagree. SBA's 13 CFR 125.3 still prints $750,000 for the subcontracting-plan threshold [704]. The codified FAR allows an 8(a) sole-source award up to $8.5 million for manufacturing codes and $5.5 million otherwise, while 13 CFR 124.506 prints $7,000,000 and $4,500,000 and SBA's program page gave $7 million and $4.5 million [338](#cite:338) [331](#cite:331) [310](#cite:310). The SBIR statute was amended on April 13, 2026, and [SBIR.gov](#term:sbir-gov) still posts the May 2023 directive [1](#cite:1) [7](#cite:7). The defense statute on [commercial solutions openings](#term:cso) dropped the word "innovative" on December 18, 2025; [DFARS](#term:dfars) Subpart 212.70 still uses it [1033](#cite:1033) [806](#cite:806) [1040](#cite:1040).

One figure is threaded down through the stack as a vertical line: the subcontracting-plan threshold reads $900,000 in the Federal Register rule and in the FAR, and the line breaks at 13 CFR 125.3, which reads $750,000 [340](#cite:340) [692](#cite:692) [704](#cite:704). A second thread does the same for the [8(a)](#term:eight-a) [sole-source](#term:sole-source) ceiling, breaking between the FAR and 13 CFR 124.506 [338](#cite:338) [331](#cite:331).

To the right, the regulation layer splits into two parallel bars, *codified FAR* and *model deviation text*, joined by a bracket labelled *same rule, two numbers*: 19.502-2 and 19.104-1 [384](#cite:384) [391](#cite:391). A small tag on the bracket lists which agencies adopted the model text for Part 19, and when [400](#cite:400) [402](#cite:402).

## How this guide uses it

Each threshold in this guide can be traced the same way. The codified FAR page gives the figure and the circular it is current to [418](#cite:418). The Federal Register rule that last changed it gives the effective date [340](#cite:340). The overhaul's deviation guide gives the model text and its issue date; it shows Part 1 issued May 2, 2025 and updated March 16, 2026 [389](#cite:389). Agency pages come last, because they can print older figures [310](#cite:310).

Where two official texts differ, the record prints both under *conflicts* and neither is smoothed away. Every *pending change* carries a status word: proposed, announced, class-deviation, final or pending-implementation. Chapter 8 lists what moved in 2025 and 2026, and chapter 9 explains how the sources were read.


Citations in this guide use the codified FAR numbers. The overhaul's numbers are recorded as pending changes, for example postaward [debriefings](#term:debriefing) at 15.301-1 in place of 15.506 [577](#cite:577).
